Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. setwd() calls were found in 1 code file.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 6 code files, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 163 columns across 3 data files.

Issues Identified

34 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 3 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

Files are missing from your deposit.

  • BoostrapMediationSimulation.R reads iorw.R.

The script stops at the line that reads the file.

  1. Find the file on your computer.
  2. Add it to the deposit, in the folder where the script looks for it.
  3. If you cannot share it, for example for privacy reasons, say so in the README, and explain where readers can get it and where to put it.

A file may have been renamed.

  • HPIcasestudy.R reads HPI2.csv; your deposit holds hpi.csv.

Check whether they are the same file. If so, use one name in both the script and the deposit.

A package could not be installed.

  • Aggregated_SpatialMediationCal.R needs rgdal.

rgdal was removed from CRAN in 2023 and can no longer be installed. Replace it with sf or terra, which do the same work, and check that your results stay the same.

A script downloads data while it runs.

  • CalSimDifferentScales.R
  • DiffComboTotMedEffects.R

Online files can move, change or disappear. Save the downloaded files, add them to the deposit, and let the script read the saved copies.

Other problems in the files

  • Aggregated_SpatialMediationCal.R calls setwd(), which sets the folder the script runs in. We replaced the call with one that does nothing, so the script ran from the top folder of the project. A folder on your own computer does not exist on another; paths written from the project’s top folder work everywhere.

Comparison with the paper

We found no statistical tests in the paper to compare with the output of the code.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 6 R code files.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), source() calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

Order File Runs after Basis
1 BoostrapMediationSimulation.R — none
2 CalSim.R — none
3 Aggregated_SpatialMediationCal.R CalSim.R dependency
4 CalSimDifferentScales.R CalSim.R dependency
5 DiffComboTotMedEffects.R CalSim.R dependency
6 HPIcasestudy.R — none

File paths

The data paths in the code to files the repository holds work as deposited, but 6 paths name a file the repository does not hold: zip_gps.csv, iorw.r, medgformula.r, hpi2.csv, ces_nodemo.csv, census_tracts_2020.csv. 6 data paths were built at runtime with sprintf()/paste()/file.path() instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author’s own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.

Missing inputs

1 input file the code reads is in the deposit but not usable as named: too large to download, inside an archive, or under a similar name.

File Status Reason
hpi2.csv absent referenced file is not present in the repository, but a similarly-named file exists: hpi.csv

Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 3 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: zip_gps.csv, ces_nodemo.csv, census_tracts_2020.csv.

They also run 2 scripts that are not in the deposit: iorw.r, medgformula.r.

Files not run on their own

1 file only defines functions, so running it on its own says nothing: a function counts when a script uses it. These files are not counted as scripts. 0 are used by no script in the deposit.

File Used by
CalSim.R Aggregated_SpatialMediationCal.R, CalSimDifferentScales.R, DiffComboTotMedEffects.R

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 6 scripts: 0 ran without error, 2 errored, 0 timed out, 1 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 1 was run by another script with source(). Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. 2 scripts need the internet, which is off during the run: CalSimDifferentScales.R, DiffComboTotMedEffects.R. Keeping what they download in the deposit solves this. 1 script uses an object or function that only another script defines, so in the second run that script was loaded first, in the same session: DiffComboTotMedEffects.R after CalSim.R. Such a script should source() the other itself, since it does not run on its own.

a script hit an object '...' not found error, indicating it expected a variable another script defines. We inferred which script supplies it and re-ordered so that script runs first, and re-ran once. The outcomes above are from that corrected run.

Aggregated_SpatialMediationCal.R dependency_unavailable dependency_unavailable 8.7

Dependency-unavailable errors

1 script could not run because its own dependency is unavailable — the package failed to install from both live CRAN and the CRAN Archive (or a GitHub/URL source could not be resolved). This is an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so it does not force the traffic light red.

File
Aggregated_SpatialMediationCal.R

setwd() in the code

1 script calls setwd(). This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after ignoring a setwd() that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed.

File setwd() removed Path(s) it set
Aggregated_SpatialMediationCal.R 1 ~/Library/Mobile Documents/comappleCloudDocs/Mediation Analysis

Run by another script

1 script is run by another script with source(), so it was not run on its own: each script runs in a fresh R process, and on its own a sourced script lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first. Its outcome is part of the sourcing script’s outcome.

Ethics Approval Check

We did not detect an ethics approval statement, and this paper does not appear to involve live data collection from human or animal participants. Ethics approval is typically not required for theoretical work, simulations, reviews, meta-analyses, or secondary analyses of published data.

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.
